'''Xu Guangxian''' ({{zh|s=徐光宪}}; November 7, 1920 – April 28, 2015), also known as '''Kwang-hsien Hsu''', was a Chinese chemist and professor at [[Peking University]]. He was an academician of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] who is respected for his contributions in both theoretical and experimental chemistry.<ref name="Preface"/><ref name="Holeung"/> He is a former president of the [[Chinese Chemical Society (Beijing)|Chinese Chemical Society]], and is known as "The Father of Chinese Rare Earths Chemistry".<ref name="Zhu Jing">{{cite book |author=Zhu Jing |title=Xu Guangxian: Father of Chinese Rare Earths Chemistry |date=January 1, 2012 |publisher=China Science and Technology Press|edition=Chinese }}</ref><ref name="Holeung">{{cite web |title=PROFILE OF XU GUANGXIAN |url=http://www.hlhl.org.cn/english/showsub.asp?id=696 |website=The Holeung Ho Lee Foundation |access-date=23 May 2019 |date=2006 |archive-date=October 3, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111003005420/http://www.hlhl.org.cn/english/showsub.asp?id=696 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Xu was born in [[Shaoxing]], [[Zhejiang]]<ref name="Holeung"/> on November 7, 1920.<ref name="CPC">{{cite web |title=State Supreme Science and Technology Award of China |url=http://cpcchina.chinadaily.com.cn/2013-01/22/content_16156854.htm |website=CPC Encyclopedia |access-date=28 May 2019 |archive-date=June 16, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210616234755/https://cpcchina.chinadaily.com.cn/2013-01/22/content_16156854.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> He entered Hangzhou Advanced Industrial Vocational School in Zhejiang<ref name="Gu Weiming"/> (now part of [[Zhejiang University of Technology]]).<ref name="ZUT">{{cite web |title=History |url=http://www.wsc.zjut.edu.cn/zjuten/BigClass.jsp?bigclassid=1&sid=70 |website=Zhejiang University of Technology |access-date=29 May 2019 |archive-date=September 30, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150930221834/http://www.wsc.zjut.edu.cn/zjuten/BigClass.jsp?bigclassid=1&sid=70 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Due to the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]], the students and faculty were relocated to an advanced industrial school in [[Ningbo]], where Xu graduated in 1939.<ref name="Gu Weiming"/>

In 1940 Xu entered Jiaotong University in [[Shanghai]] (now known as [[Shanghai Jiao Tong University]], SJTU).<ref name="SJTU"/> Again, there was disruption at the university because of the war.<ref>{{cite web |title=About Us |url=http://scce.sjtu.edu.cn/en/xygk.php?t=5 |website=School of Chemistry, Shanghai Jiao Tong University |access-date=29 May 2019}}</ref> Xu received his B.Sc. in 1944.<ref name="SJTU">{{cite web |title=Xu Guangxian |url=http://en.sjtu.edu.cn/spotlight/alumni-spotlight/da2009/xu-guangxian/ |website=Shanghai Jiao Tong University |access-date=28 May 2019 |date=2010 |archive-date=May 28, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190528194117/http://en.sjtu.edu.cn/spotlight/alumni-spotlight/da2009/xu-guangxian/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 1945, Xu Guangxian worked as a teaching assistant at SJTU, with professor Gu Jidong.<ref name="SJTU"/>
He married one of his classmates, chemist [[Gao Xiaoxia]] in 1946.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Women of China|location=Beijing |date=1998 |page=30 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8payAAAAIAAJ}}</ref>

Xu and Gao passed national examinations for studying abroad in 1946. Xu traveled to the United States in 1948 to attend the graduate school of [[Washington University in St. Louis]]. After ranking first in a probationary summer class at [[Columbia University]] in [[New York City]], he was able to transfer to Columbia.<ref name="Gu Weiming"/> There he studied quantum chemistry with a minor in physics from 1948 to 1951.<ref name="Preface"/> He also worked as a teaching assistant, enabling Gao Xiaoxia to join him and study [[analytical chemistry]] at [[New York University]].<ref name="Gu Weiming"/>

Xu received his MS in 1949 and his [[PhD]] in 1951<ref name="Klinger">{{cite book |last1=Klinger |first1=Julie Michelle |title=Rare earth frontiers : from terrestrial subsoils to lunar landscapes |date=2017 |publisher=Cornell University Press |location=Ithaca, NY|isbn=978-1501714603 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JpFFDwAAQBAJ |pages=100–102 }}</ref><ref name="Hepeng Jia">{{cite journal |author1=Hepeng Jia |author2=Lihui Di |title=Xu Guangxian: a chemical life |journal=Chemistry World |date=31 March 2009 |url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/news/xu-guangxian-a-chemical-life/3004349.article |access-date=23 May 2019}}</ref> working with Charles O. Beckmann.<ref name="Rasmussen">{{cite book |author-last=Mainz|author-first=Vera V.|chapter=Chapter 5: History of the modern chemistry doctoral program in mainland China|editor-last1=Rasmussen |editor-first1=Seth C. |title=Igniting the chemical ring of fire : historical evolution of the chemical communities of the Pacific Rim |date=2018 |publisher=World Scientific |location=New Jersey |isbn=9781786344540 |pages=115–119 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lNFKDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA115 |access-date=23 May 2019}}</ref> His thesis in [[quantum chemistry]] was "Optically Active Quantum Chemical Theory".<ref name="Gu Weiming">{{cite web |author=Gu Weiming |title=Recall Father of China's Rare Earth, Alumnus of SJTU Academician Xu Guangxian |url=http://en.sjtu.edu.cn/news/recall-father-of-chinas-rare-earth-alumnus-of-sjtu-academician-xu-guangxian/ |access-date=28 May 2019 |website=Shanghai Jiao Tong University |date=April 28, 2015 |archive-date=May 29, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190529124434/http://en.sjtu.edu.cn/news/recall-father-of-chinas-rare-earth-alumnus-of-sjtu-academician-xu-guangxian/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> In February 1949, he became a member of the [[Phi Lambda Upsilon]] National Honorary Chemical Society (ΦΛΥ). In October 1950, Xu became a member of [[Sigma Xi]] (ΣΞ).<ref name="Gu Weiming"/>

Meanwhile, in China, the [[Chinese Civil War]] resulted in the formation of the [[People's Republic of China]] in 1949. The [[Korean War]] broke out in June, 1950. Soon after, the United States government passed an act forbidding Chinese citizens who were studying in America from returning to China.<ref name="Yelong Han">{{cite journal |author=Yelong Han |title=An Untold Story: American Policy toward Chinese Students in the United States, 1949–1955 |journal=The Journal of American-East Asian Relations |date=1993 |volume=2 |issue=1 (Special Issue: The Impact of the Korean War) |pages=77–99 |jstor=23612667 |doi=10.1163/187656193X00095 }}</ref> Concerned that they might not be allowed to return home if they waited until Gao Xiaoxia received her Ph.D., Xu Guangxian and Gao Xiaoxia applied for short-term visas to China. On April 15, 1951, they left for China on the [[USS General W. H. Gordon (AP-117)|USS ''General Gordon'']], one of the last three cruisers to leave for China before the American ban went into effect.<ref name="SJTU"/>

==Career==
After returning to [[China]] in 1951, Xu became an associate professor at the Department of Chemistry of [[Peking University]]. By autumn 1952, he held professorships in both the Department of Chemistry and the Department of Technical Physics. Xu held various directorships at the university. He worked primarily in the areas of quantum chemistry and chemical bonding theory. He studied the bonding characteristics of molecules and proposed a formula relating the order of filling of atomic orbital levels to the grouping of elements into periods in the periodic table. This led to greater understanding of the [[lanthanides]] and [[actinides]].<ref name="Preface"/>

Xu became the department dean in 1956 and directed the department of [[radiation chemistry]].<ref name="Peng Kuang">{{cite news |author=Peng Kuang |title=Chemist's contributions worth their weight in gold |url=http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2009-01/10/content_7384665.htm |access-date=28 May 2019 |work=China Daily |date=January 10, 2009}}</ref> Xu was involved in the Chinese [[nuclear weapons]] development program, in which he played a role in separating and extracting elements for nuclear fuels. In particular, he did experimental research on the separation of [[Uranium-235]] and [[Uranium-238]].<ref name="Peng Kuang"/><ref>[http://bk.baidu.com/view/24216.htm 百度百科]{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} 1959年2月 开始从事铀-235同位素分离方法的研究，讲授核燃料化学。</ref> After 1966, when the [[Cultural Revolution]] began, Xu's department stopped doing atomic research.<ref name="Hurst"/>

During the [[Cultural Revolution]], Xu and his wife Gao Xiaoxia were accused of spying for the [[Kuomintang]] and sent to a [[labor camp]] from 1969 to 1972.<ref name="Rasmussen"/><ref name="Hurst">{{cite web|url=http://www.iags.org/rareearth0310hurst.pdf|title=China's Rare Earth Elements Industry: What Can the West Learn?|first1=Cindy |last1=Hurst|date=March 2010|work=Institute for the Analysis of Global Security (IAGS)]}}</ref>{{rp|8}}

[[File:Praseodymium1.jpg|thumb|right|The element praseodymium]]

When he returned to Peking University in 1972, Xu was asked to change his field of study to the extraction of [[praseodymium]], a [[rare earth element]].<ref name="Rasmussen"/><ref name="Preface"/> During the 1970s, Xu studied the theoretical basis and design for solvent extraction, developed mathematical models, and made important contributions towards the development of separation processes for rare earth elements.<ref name="Hurst"/><ref name="Evans">{{cite book |last1=Evans |first1=C. H. |title=Episodes from the History of the Rare Earth Elements |date=December 6, 2012 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |isbn=978-94-009-0287-9 |pages=137 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EFzuCAAAQBAJ |access-date=23 May 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Zhu Jing |title=Study on scientific thought and method of Xu Guangxian |journal=Chemistry Bulletin / Huaxue Tongbao |date=May 18, 2012 |volume=75 |issue=3 |pages=284–288}}</ref> Gao Xiaoxia's development of microanalytical techniques in [[polarography]] contributed to the success of Xu's research.<ref name="Hurst"/><ref name="Rasmussen"/> Xu developed the process of countercurrent extraction (also known as series extraction or cascade extraction)<ref name="Rasmussen"/><ref name="Hurst"/> and substantially reduced both the time needed to extract materials, and their resulting cost.<ref name="Peng Kuang"/>

Xu founded the Research Center of Rare Earth Chemistry as of 1986 and was essential in establishing the State Key Laboratory of Rare Earth Materials Chemistry and Applications in 1989.<ref name="Holeung"/><ref name="Preface"/> He served as director and as chairman of its academic committee.<ref name="Preface"/><ref name="Goldman">{{Cite journal|last=Goldman|first=Joanne Abel|date=April 2014|title=The U.S. Rare Earth Industry: Its Growth and Decline|journal=Journal of Policy History|volume=26|issue=2|pages=139–166|doi=10.1017/s0898030614000013|s2cid=154319330|issn=0898-0306}}</ref>

In 2005, Xu Guangxian raised concerns about the mining of thorium in the [[Baotou]] area, where mine wastes were released into the [[Yellow River]].<ref name="Hurst"/><ref name="Emergency">{{cite journal |author1=Xu Guangxian |title=An Emergency Call for the Protection of Thorium and Rare Earth Resources at Baiyun Erbo and the Prevention of Radioactive Contamination of the Yellow River and Baotou |publisher=Chinese Academy of Sciences |date=October 20, 2005}}</ref> The Yellow River is a source of drinking water for an estimated 150 million people, so radioactive contamination is a very serious issue.<ref name="Yellow River">{{cite news |title=China's dilemma: how to mine rare earths whilst protecting reserves and the environment |url=http://www.asianews.it/news-en/China%E2%80%99s-dilemma:-how-to-mine-rare-earths-whilst-protecting-reserves-and-the-environment-21039.html |access-date=30 May 2019 |work=Asia News |date=March 15, 2011}}</ref> Xu has suggested that the Chinese develop stocks of rare earths to stave off shortages of rare earths.<ref>{{cite news |title=Chinese Rare Earth Expert Calls for Immediate Stockpiling |work=Metal-Pages |date=November 2, 200}}</ref>

Xu published more than 500 reviewed papers<ref name="Preface"/> and several books. These included ''Principle of Extraction Chemistry'', ''Rare Earth Solvent Extraction'', ''The Structure of Matter'' and ''The Basic Principles of Quantum Chemistry and Ab-initio Calculation''.<ref name="Preface"/> Xu has supervised hundreds of students.<ref name="Rasmussen"/>

==Awards and honors==
* Xu has twice received China's [[State Natural Science Award]] (Second Class and Third Class, 1987); twice received the [[State Science and Technology Progress Award]] (Second Class, 1998; Third Class, 1991); and received the [[Ho Leung Ho Lee Prize]] for Scientific and Technological Progress in 1994.<ref name="Holeung"/>
* Xu received the 2008 [[State Preeminent Science and Technology Award]]. It was presented to him at the [[Great Hall of the People]] in Beijing, on January 9, 2009, by [[Hu Jintao]]. Xu was also congratulated by [[Wen Jiabao]].<ref name="Peng Kuang"/><ref name="Hepeng Jia"/> The award is considered to be China's equivalent to the [[Nobel Prize]].<ref name="Hurst"/>
* In 2009, Xu Guangxian, [[Qian Xuesen]], [[Zhang Guangdou]], and [[Wu Wenjun]] were honored with the inaugural SJTU Outstanding Alumni Lifetime Achievement Award from Shanghai Jiao Tong University.<ref name="Xu Yang">{{cite web |author=Xu Yang |title=SJTU Outstanding Alumni Lifetime Achievement Award Winner Zhang Guangdou Passed Away |url=http://en.sjtu.edu.cn/news/sjtu-outstanding-alumni-lifetime-achievement-award-winner-zhang-guangdou-passed-away/ |website=Shanghai Jiao Tong University |access-date=29 May 2019 |date=June 22, 2013 |archive-date=May 29, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190529025748/http://en.sjtu.edu.cn/news/sjtu-outstanding-alumni-lifetime-achievement-award-winner-zhang-guangdou-passed-away/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Gu Weiming"/>
* Asteroid [[345871 Xuguangxian]], discovered by astronomers with the [[PMO NEO Survey Program]] at Purple Mountain Observatory in 2007, was named in his memory.<ref name="MPC-object" /> The official {{MoMP|345871|naming citation}} was published by the [[Minor Planet Center]] on January 9, 2020 ({{small|[[Minor Planet Circulars|M.P.C.]] 120070}}).<ref name="MPC-Circulars-Archive" />

Xu died in [[Beijing]] on April 28, 2015, at age 94.<ref name="Gu Weiming"/><ref name="Obituary">{{cite web |author=Jin Panzhu |title=In Memory of Master Xu Guangxian MAY 09 2015 |url=http://newsen.pku.edu.cn/news_events/news/people/3675.htm |access-date=23 May 2019 |website=Peking University}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author1=刘原革|script-title=zh:中国稀土之父徐光宪院士逝世 曾获国家最高科学技术奖|url=http://www.chinanews.com/gn/2015/04-28/7240402.shtml|access-date=2015-04-28|agency=中国新闻网|date=2015-04-28|language=zh}}</ref>

== Memberships ==
* Elected to the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] in 1980<ref name="Preface">{{cite journal |author=Lemin Li |title=Preface |journal=Science in China Series B: Chemistry |date=2009 |volume=52 |issue=11 |pages=1715–1722 |url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11426-009-0286-6.pdf |access-date=29 May 2019|doi=10.1007/s11426-009-0286-6 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* President (1986―1990), [[Chinese Chemical Society (Beijing)|Chinese Chemical Society]] (CCS)<ref name="Preface"/>
* [[Vice-president]] (1980―1999), Chinese Society of Rare Earths (CSRE)<ref name="Preface"/><ref>[http://www.cs-re.org.cn/introduct.htm The Chinese Society of Rare Earths(CSRE)] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080228185631/http://www.cs-re.org.cn/introduct.htm |date=February 28, 2008 }}</ref> Honorary vice-president thereafter<ref name="Preface"/>
* [[Editor-in-chief]], ''Rare Earths'' (a 3-volume monograph on the science and technology of rare earths in China), Metallurgical Industry Press, [[Beijing]], 1995<ref>[http://www.chem.pku.edu.cn/xugx/eindex.htm Selected publications of Xu Guangxian] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080308143139/http://www.chem.pku.edu.cn/xugx/eindex.htm |date=March 8, 2008 }}</ref>
* Editor-in-chief, ''Journal of Rare Earths''<ref name="Voncken">{{cite book |last1=Voncken |first1=J.H.L. |title=The Rare Earth Elements : an Introduction |date=2016 |publisher=Springer |isbn=9783319268071 |page=111 |edition=1st. 2016 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ik9ECwAAQBAJ&pg=PA111 |access-date=23 May 2019}}</ref>
